interactive.title: The volts lost from the intake
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Eleven screens, with Back and Continue, on voltage drop from the origin to the load. Screen 1, Do you still have it? (your slides p.41): “A supply is given as 395 V. A submain feeding a second board has a calculated voltage drop of 10 V, and a radial power circuit from that board 9.8 V. Does the circuit comply?” Three choices, in this order: “Yes: 19.8 V is inside 5% of 400 V, 20.00 V”; “Yes: the radial's 9.8 V is inside the limit on its own”; “No: 19.8 V is over 5% of 395 V, 19.75 V”. Right: “Still there.”, the working 10 + 9.8 = 19.8 V; 395 × 0.05 = 19.75 V, so it does not comply;[^7] a line each on the slips. Two buttons: Refresh the why (screen 2), Skip to the practice (screen 8). Wrong, the first: with 395 V given, your slides take 5% of 395 V.[^6] Wrong, the second: the limit covers every drop from the intake, the submain's 10 V too.[^10] Then the right working and on to screen 2. Read: 10 + 9.8 = 19.8 V, over 5% of the given 395 V, 19.75 V: it does not comply.

Screen 2, What it is for: the cable's resistance uses up some of the supply's voltage on the way, and the load gets what is left: VD = mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000,[^1][^2] within Table 4Ab's limits, as your slides give them (p.38): lighting up to 3%, 6.9 V single-phase and 12 V three-phase;[^3] other circuits up to 5%, 11.5 V and 20 V,[^4] from the origin to the most distant point of the circuit.[^8] In red, if it is skipped or worked on one cable only: the load runs on less than it was designed for. A heater's power falls with the square of its voltage,[^88] and a motor draws more current to keep its torque.[^89] Your slides' 3 kW heater on 85 m of 1.5 mm² drops 32.14 V,[^35] nearly three times the 11.50 V allowed.[^4] Read: VD = mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000, within 3% (lighting) or 5% (other circuits) from the origin to the far end.

Screen 3, The why: the drop from the origin. The picture, left to right, short labels: Origin, Submain, Board, Heater circuit, Heater; under it the voltage along the path, a step down across the submain and a slope along the heater circuit; below 218.50 V (230 V less the 11.50 V limit) a band shaded red. The course joins two of your slides' examples (its own combination): a 10 V submain drop (p.41, taken here as three-phase) and, from that board, the single-phase 3 kW heater (p.42), 13.04 A in 6.0 mm², 7.3 mV/A/m (Table 4D1B, your copy p.449, column 3).[^39] No supply voltage is given, so the origin is the nominal 230 V. The submain's drop is line to line and the heater circuit runs line to neutral, a √3 smaller, so the formula sheet divides it by √3 before adding:[^11] 10.00 ÷ √3 = 5.77 V, leaving 224.23 V at the board. A slider, Heater circuit length, 0 to 120 m in 5 m steps, opening at 85 m. Readouts: Heater circuit's drop (7.3 × 13.04 × length ÷ 1000); Total from the origin (5.77 V plus that); Limit, 11.50 V.[^4] At 85 m: 8.09 V,[^14] inside the limit on its own; total 13.86 V, over, and the heater's 216.14 V sits in the red band. At 60 m: 5.71 V, total 11.48 V, inside; at 65 m: 6.19 V, total 11.96 V, over. The total crosses the limit near 60 m; the heater circuit alone stays inside it to 120 m (11.42 V). Under it, why: the heater gets what the origin's voltage leaves after every cable it is fed through, so the drops add.[^9][^10] Read: at 85 m the heater circuit drops 8.09 V; with the submain's 5.77 V the total is 13.86 V, over 11.50 V; it reaches the limit near 60 m.

Screen 4, Check: “A three-phase motor circuit has a calculated voltage drop of 7.2 V. Its board is fed by a three-phase submain with a calculated drop of 9.0 V. No supply voltage is given. What is the total, and does it comply?” Choices: “12.40 V: the submain's drop ÷ √3 first, so it complies”; “16.20 V, over 11.50 V: it does not comply”; “16.20 V, inside 20.00 V: it complies”. Right, the third: 7.2 + 9.0 = 16.20 V, three-phase all the way, against 5% of 400 V.[^64][^4] Wrong, 12.40 V (9.0 ÷ √3 = 5.20 V; 7.2 + 5.20): the ÷ √3 is for a three-phase submain feeding a single-phase circuit;[^11] this load is three-phase. Wrong, 11.50 V: that is 5% of 230 V; a three-phase circuit takes 5% of the three-phase voltage.[^64] Read: 7.2 + 9.0 = 16.20 V, inside 20.00 V.

Screen 5, Worked example, a line at each press (Work each step yourself first, then press Show), your slides p.42: a 3 kW heater, 70 °C thermoplastic singles, 35 °C, Reference Method B, 85 m.[^33] Ib = 3000 ÷ 230 = 13.04 A (lesson 3), Ca 0.94,[^34] 1.5 mm². VD = 29 × 13.04 × 85 ÷ 1000 = 32.14 V,[^35] over 11.50 V (the slides print 32.1 V, cut short). Chasing the volt drop: a bigger CSA, and the sum again, until it complies.[^13] The most mV/A/m that can pass at 85 m: 11.50 × 1000 ÷ (13.04 × 85) = 10.37 (rounded down). 4.0 mm², 11 mV/A/m (Table 4D1B, your copy p.449, column 3),[^38] is over it: 11 × 13.04 × 85 ÷ 1000 = 12.19 V, fails. 6.0 mm², 7.3 mV/A/m:[^39] 7.3 × 13.04 × 85 ÷ 1000 = 8.09 V, passes.[^14] Last line, the slides' next question (p.43): the 6.0 mm² still carries just 13.04 A,[^29] and Table 4D1A rates it at 41 A.[^28] Read: 1.5 mm² 32.14 V and 4.0 mm² 12.19 V fail; 6.0 mm² 8.09 V passes; the most that can pass is 10.37 mV/A/m.

Screen 6, The why, refined (why piece C): a lightly loaded cable. Opening text: Appendix 4's mV/A/m are for the conductor at its maximum operating temperature, 70 °C or 90 °C, reached only at full load.[^15] Current heats a conductor, raising its resistance and so the drop;[^17] at lower loads its temperature and resistance are lower.[^16] Ct corrects the drop for it. The picture: the slides' heater, 13.04 A on 85 m; a named choice, Cable: 1.5 mm², 4.0 mm², 6.0 mm², opening on 6.0 mm²; a switch, Apply Ct, opening off; a bar for Ib as a share of It; two bars in volts, the drop (red when over) and the 11.50 V limit. Under it, as a fraction on two lines: Ct = (230 + tp − (Ca² Cg² − Ib²/It²)(tp − 30)) ÷ (230 + tp),[^19] tp the conductor's maximum operating temperature, 70 °C for PVC (thermoplastic), 90 °C for XLPE,[^20] Ca the ambient temperature factor,[^21] It the tabulated current rating.[^23] One way to picture Ib²/It²: heat goes with the square of the current, so 13.04 A in a cable rated 41 A makes about a tenth of its full-load heat. Here tp 70 °C, Ca 0.94 (0.94² = 0.8836), Cg 1. Readouts: Ib ÷ It; Ct; Drop. Each cable's working is in the case file (l5.ct.15, l5.ct.4, l5.ct.6). 1.5 mm², 29 mV/A/m, It 17.5 A (Table 4D1A, your copy p.448, column 4):[^152] Ct 0.96, 30.85 V; near its rating a cable gains little. 4.0 mm², 11 mV/A/m, It 32 A:[^36] (13.04 ÷ 32)² = 0.1661; 0.8836 − 0.1661 = 0.7175; × 40 = 28.70; (300 − 28.70) ÷ 300 = 0.9043, Ct 0.90; 12.19 × 0.90 = 10.97 V, inside. 6.0 mm², 7.3 mV/A/m, It 41 A:[^37] Ct 0.90, 7.28 V. The moment to see: Ct on with 4.0 mm², and its bar falls under the limit: with Ct a smaller CSA than 6.0 mm² may pass.[^31] A box headed Debated: the formula is as a reader quoted it, attributing it to BS 7671[^19] (check it against Appendix 4 in your copy); one IET forum contributor counts only the ambient temperature and grouping factors in it,[^32] so Ci is left out here. Ct earns its keep where Ib is well below It and few correction factors apply;[^24] with a grouping factor of 0.78 alone it comes to about 0.99.[^30] Read: in 4.0 mm² the heater circuit drops 12.19 V, over 11.50 V; with Ct 0.90, 10.97 V, inside.

Screen 7, The why, refined: a known power factor. From 25 mm² up the tables give r, x and z;[^40][^42] with no known power factor z is acceptable,[^18] with one, r and x are used.[^41] The picture: the r drop as an arrow along the current, the x drop a quarter-cycle ahead of it at right angles, z their sum as the long side; the load's voltage as a line at the angle φ from the current, each drop's shadow along it. A slider, Power factor, 0.50 to 1.00 in steps of 0.05, opening at 0.80 (the showroom motor's). The cable: 25 mm² 90 °C singles in conduit, three-phase, r 1.60, x 0.27, z 1.65 mV/A/m (Table 4E1B, your copy p.459).[^55] Readouts: sin φ = √(1 − cos² φ);[^49] Drop per amp per metre, r × cos φ + x × sin φ;[^48] z, 1.65. At 1.00: 1.60. At 0.80: 1.60 × 0.8 + 0.27 × 0.6 = 1.28 + 0.16 = 1.44 mV/A/m, about 13% under z. At 0.50 (sin φ 0.87): 0.80 + 0.23 = 1.03. Why: the r drop is in step with the current and the x drop a quarter-cycle ahead, so only their parts along the load's voltage take away from its size. Taking z as if all of it lay along the voltage may give a drop higher than the actual one;[^45] r and x allow an accurate assessment for loads with a large inductive element,[^46] so a circuit may conform without being upsized.[^50] This lesson does not combine Ct with r and x. Read: at power factor 0.8, 1.60 × 0.8 + 0.27 × 0.6 = 1.44 mV/A/m, against z's 1.65.

Screen 8, Section A, question 1 (g): the scenario panel, and parts (a) to (f) carried forward. Given, each the course's own: the motor fed from DBP2, about 11.4 m along the walls on plan (approximate; a real design adds the vertical runs, guide p.5); DBP2 to the starter, 2.5 mm² 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit, one three-phase circuit, 16 mV/A/m (Table 4E1B, your copy p.459, column 6);[^53] starter to motor, part (f)'s six 1.5 mm² singles, 3.0 m, a practice value (measure the real run), 31 mV/A/m for two cables single-phase (column 3);[^54] the DBP2 submain's three-phase drop, 4.00 V, a practice value. The leg: in delta running the windings are three single-phase loads,[^59] each fed through two of the six conductors, one at each end,[^124] carrying the winding current, 13.33 A (part b). The course takes its drop as 31 × 13.33 × 3.0 ÷ 1000, line to line, added to the rest: its own reading, not BS 7671's, and debated: a forum poster multiplies by √3 as well,[^62] 2.15 V here. “(g) Determine the actual voltage drop of the motor circuit, from the intake to the motor.” A typed answer (part 1g): 16 × 23.08 × 11.4 ÷ 1000 = 4.21 V; 31 × 13.33 × 3.0 ÷ 1000 = 1.24 V; 4.00 + 4.21 + 1.24 = 9.45 V (on practice values), inside 5% of 400 V, 20.00 V:[^4] 2.36%. No ÷ √3: the motor is three-phase.[^64] Accepted too, each with its own line: 10.36 V (the forum's reading; the line current, 31 × 23.08 × 3.0 ÷ 1000, gives the same 2.15 V, though each conductor carries the winding current[^63]) and 9.15 V (with Ct). Slips: 5.45 V (the submain left out[^10]); 8.21 V (the leg left out: all lengths count, guide p.5); 7.76 V (the submain ÷ √3, 2.31 V: that is for a single-phase circuit[^11]). After two misses, the working. Then a fold, Refined with Ct (working: l5.A.1g.ct): the 2.5 mm² cable carries 23.08 A of its 28 A (Table 4E1A, column 5);[^56] tp 90 °C, Ca 1.00 (lesson 3's practice value), Cg 1: Ct 0.94, 3.96 V; the leg, Cg 0.80, It 20 A:[^57] Ct 0.96, 1.19 V; in all 9.15 V, not needed since 9.45 V passes. Under 25 mm² the power factor does not enter.[^40] Read: 4.00 + 4.21 + 1.24 = 9.45 V (on practice values), inside 20.00 V.

Screen 9, Section B: “Explain why a cable carrying well under its rating drops less voltage than Appendix 4's mV/A/m gives, and how a designer can take credit for it.” Written, marked against five points (any three make a full answer); one more go, then the model answer.

Screen 10, Section A, changed numbers: “A single-phase power circuit, 32 m of 1.5 mm² 90 °C singles in conduit (31 mV/A/m), Ib 9 A, is fed from a sub-board whose three-phase submain drops 7.5 V. No supply voltage is given. Determine the total voltage drop from the origin.”[^54] A typed answer: 31 × 9 × 32 ÷ 1000 = 8.93 V; 7.5 ÷ √3 = 4.33 V;[^11] 4.33 + 8.93 = 13.26 V, over 11.50 V: it fails, though the circuit alone would pass. Accepted: 13.27 V (√3 as 1.73, as your slides take it).[^158] Slips: 16.43 V (no ÷ √3), 21.92 V (7.5 × √3 = 12.99 V), 8.93 V (the submain left out[^10]). Read: 8.93 V; 7.5 ÷ √3 = 4.33 V; 4.33 + 8.93 = 13.26 V, over 11.50 V.

Screen 11, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson. The line under screens 3 to 8 and 10: figures from your slides, formula sheet, assignment and copy of BS 7671; practice values marked; each line worked from the rounded figures before it.

explain.text:
Voltage drop is the voltage the cables use up on the way to the load: the load gets what is left. Your slides count it as mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000, where mV/A/m is the millivolts dropped for every ampere of design current for every metre of conductor,[^1][^2] and they allow up to 3% of the supply for lighting and 5% for other circuits,[^3][^4] taken of the supply voltage you were given where one is given.[^6]

The limit runs from the origin of the installation to the most distant point of the circuit,[^8] because the load gets what the origin's voltage leaves after every cable it is fed through. So the submain's drop is added to the final circuit's,[^9] and a final circuit that passes on its own can still fail: on your slides' 395 V supply, 10 V in the submain and 9.8 V in the circuit make 19.8 V, over the 19.75 V allowed.[^7] A three-phase submain's drop is a line-to-line figure. Where it feeds a single-phase circuit, which runs line to neutral, a √3 smaller, the formula sheet divides it by √3 before adding;[^11] where the load is three-phase too, the drops stay three-phase and are judged against 3% or 5% of the three-phase voltage.[^64]

Two refinements can bring a narrow fail inside. The tables' mV/A/m are worked for the conductor at its maximum operating temperature, which it reaches only at full load.[^15] Current heats a conductor and a hotter conductor has more resistance,[^17] so a cable carrying well under its rating runs cooler and drops less,[^16] and a factor, [[Ct]], corrects the drop for it. Your slides' heater cable, chased up to 6.0 mm², still carries just 13.04 A of the 41 A it is rated for,[^29][^28] so it drops less than its 8.09 V, and with Ct the smaller 4.0 mm² may pass.[^27][^31] From 25 mm² up the tables give r, x and z.[^40] With a known power factor, the r drop is in step with the current and the x drop a quarter of a cycle ahead of it, so only their parts along the load's voltage take away from it: (mV/A/m)r × cos φ + (mV/A/m)x × sin φ.[^48] Using z alone may give a drop higher than the actual one.[^45] This is a simplified picture: taking the drops' shadows along the voltage is very close to the exact figure while the drop is small beside the supply voltage.

**Add every drop from the intake to the far end and judge the total against 3% or 5% of the voltage you were given; where it fails narrowly, a lightly loaded cable's Ct, or with a known power factor its r and x, may show that it passes.**[^10][^6][^31][^41]

analogy.text: Think of a ship's fresh-water main. The pressure at a shower on the far deck is the pump's pressure less what is lost in every length of pipe on the way, the ring main as well as the branch. A branch that loses little on its own can still leave too little at the shower once the ring main has taken its share, so the loss is judged from the pump, not from the branch's own valve.
analogy.breaks: A pipe's loss climbs faster than its flow, while a cable's drop is in proportion to its current. And an AC cable's reactance drops voltage out of step with the current, which a pipe has no counterpart for, so the r and x refinement has no water version.

practice.text:
- Work Ib at the voltage given (lesson 1), then each cable's drop: mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000,[^2] with mV/A/m from the Appendix 4 voltage-drop table for that cable and its installation.[^52]
- Add every drop from the intake to the end of the circuit, submain and final circuit,[^10][^9] and every length of the run, the drops into and out of ceiling voids included (project guide p.5).
- A three-phase submain feeding a single-phase circuit: divide the submain's drop by √3 before adding.[^11] A three-phase load: keep every drop three-phase.[^64]
- Judge the total against 3% (lighting) or 5% (other circuits) of the voltage you were given;[^3][^4][^6] where none is given, against the nominal 230 V or 400 V (formula sheet step 7).
- Fails? Chase it: a bigger CSA, and the sum again, until it complies.[^13] Then, for a cable carrying well under its rating, try Ct;[^24] at 25 mm² and over with a known power factor, use r and x.[^41]

**Rule of thumb:** the most mV/A/m that can pass is the limit × 1000 ÷ (Ib × L); the first cable under it is the one to try. Ct earns most where Ib is well below It and few correction factors apply;[^24] with a grouping factor of 0.78 and nothing else it comes to about 0.99.[^30]

**Worked example:** the showroom motor, part 1(g), on practice values (the DBP2 submain's 4.00 V and the 3.0 m leg). DBP2 to the starter: 16 × 23.08 × 11.4 ÷ 1000 = 4.21 V (2.5 mm², Table 4E1B column 6).[^53] The leg, at the winding current, 31 × 13.33 × 3.0 ÷ 1000 = 1.24 V (1.5 mm², column 3),[^54] the course's own reading of a debated step.[^62] Total 4.00 + 4.21 + 1.24 = 9.45 V, inside 5% of 400 V, 20.00 V,[^4] with no ÷ √3, since the motor is three-phase.[^64]

**Common mistakes**
- Checking the final circuit on its own: the limit covers every drop from the intake.[^10]
- Taking 5% of 400 V when the supply is given as 395 V.[^7]
- Dividing by √3 when the load is three-phase.[^64]
- Using z with a known power factor on 25 mm² and over: it may overstate the drop.[^45]
- Taking the Ct formula's factors as settled: the one here uses Ca and Cg, not Ci;[^32] check it against Appendix 4 in your copy.

b1.q: Explain why a cable carrying well under its rating drops less voltage than Appendix 4's mV/A/m gives, and how a designer can take credit for it.

b1.model: Appendix 4's mV/A/m values are worked for the conductor at its maximum operating temperature, 70 °C or 90 °C, which it reaches only when it carries its full load. Current heats a conductor, and a hotter conductor has more resistance, so more drop (your slides p.43). A cable carrying well under its rating, Ib well below It, runs cooler, so its resistance and its drop are lower than the table says. The designer takes credit with the factor Ct, worked from Ib and It, the maximum operating temperature and the rating factors, which multiplies the tabulated drop. It can let a smaller cable pass: your slides' heater in 4.0 mm² drops 12.19 V by the table but 10.97 V with Ct, inside the 11.50 V limit.

summary.title: Voltage drop from the intake, refined
summary.for: Enough voltage must reach the load. The drop from the origin to the far end of the circuit is kept within 3% (lighting) or 5% (other circuits) of the voltage you were given (slides p.38, 40).
summary.rule:
VD = mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000
Total = submain + final circuit, from the intake
3-phase submain, 1-phase circuit: submain ÷ √3
Limit: 3% or 5% of the voltage given (230 V or 400 V if none)
Ct = (230 + tp − (Ca² Cg² − Ib²/It²)(tp − 30)) ÷ (230 + tp)
25 mm² and up, power factor known: r × cos φ + x × sin φ

Fails? Chase it with a bigger CSA, then try Ct.
A three-phase load keeps every drop three-phase.
The Ct formula is as quoted in research: check Appendix 4 in your copy.

traps.text: Checking the final circuit on its own: the limit covers every drop from the intake to the end of the circuit.
traps.cite: Project guide p.6; formula sheet step 7

traps.text: Taking 5% of 400 V when the supply is given as 395 V: the limit is 19.75 V, not 20 V.
Dividing by √3 when the load is three-phase: the ÷ √3 is for a three-phase submain feeding a single-phase circuit.
Using z on 25 mm² and over when the power factor is known: it may overstate the drop.
traps.cite: Slides p.45; NICEIC, impedance and voltage drop, in research

traps.text: Leaving a cable chased up for voltage drop at its tabulated drop: it runs cooler, and with Ct a smaller cable may pass.
